evidence.claim: South Carolina designated it a scenic highway in 1988, prohibiting new off-premises outdoor advertising.
evidence.quote: Any new off-premises outdoor advertising is prohibited on the Ft. Johnson Road Scenic Highway after the effective date of this article.

evidence.claim: The law also protects trees larger than six inches in caliper within the right-of-way: removal requires transportation department permission on Charleston County Council’s recommendation.
evidence.quote: No trees in excess of a six-inch caliper located within the highway right-of-way of this scenic highway may be removed without the permission of the Department of Transportation upon the recommendation of the governing council of the County of Charleston.

evidence.claim: Fort Johnson’s guns helped the Confederates capture Fort Sumter in 1861.
evidence.quote: These guns were heavily relied upon during the initial Confederate capture of Fort Sumter on April 13, 1861.

evidence.claim: Confederate soldiers later buried the fort, which was uncovered in 1931.
evidence.quote: Later on in the American Civil War the fort was buried by Confederate soldiers.  In 1931 it was uncovered.

evidence.claim: The Town of James Island has never included the entire island.
evidence.quote: The town limits have never incorporated the entire island of James Island

evidence.claim: Its boundaries were central to a sequence of incorporations and court challenges beginning in 1993.
evidence.quote: Island residents incorporated the Town of James Island on January 8, 1993.

evidence.claim: Charleston challenged the first incorporation because already annexed salt marsh separated parts of the town.
evidence.quote: the parts of the new Town were not contiguous, being separated by salt marsh that it had already incorporated.

evidence.claim: After further attempts, the state Supreme Court ruled in 2011 that the incorporation law was constitutional but approximately a quarter of the town was not contiguous.
evidence.quote: It ruled that the South Carolina incorporation law used by the Town was constitutional, but that approximately 25% of the Town was not contiguous.

evidence.claim: The remedy was closure of the whole town. A fourth incorporation followed a referendum in April 2012.
evidence.quote:
Rather than remove that portion of the Town, it ordered the Town closed.
The Town was incorporated a fourth time after a referendum on April 24, 2012.

evidence.claim: Marshlands House reached James Island through relocation, not original construction here.
evidence.quote: The house was relocated in the 1960s from its original location on the site of the United States Navy Shipyard.

evidence.claim: Built in 1810, the two-and-a-half-story Federal-style plantation house stood on what became the Navy shipyard site.
evidence.quote: was built in 1810

evidence.claim: The Navy warned that the empty house would be demolished unless it could be moved using $15,000 set aside for the purpose.
evidence.quote: The Navy had announced it would have to demolish the empty house if it could not be relocated with the $15,000 the Navy had set aside for the purpose.

evidence.claim: Charleston took temporary possession, then transferred it to the College of Charleston, which moved it for preservation in the 1960s.
evidence.quote: The City of Charleston took temporary possession of the house, transferring it to the College of Charleston which relocated it for preservation to James Island.

flags: The SCDOT story-map page cited by current/material is absent. Dropped the unsupported 4.5-mile length and Folly Road starting point. The overview describes only the SCDNR-supported final approach; source evidence does not support an end-to-end itinerary or road geometry.

The statute establishes designation and roadside protections, but gives no scenic-selection rationale or road-construction history. The historical paragraph therefore follows the destination’s change in use. Tree protection is specific to the highway right-of-way and county recommendation.
SCDNR directions describe passage through a gate but do not establish unrestricted visitor access or opening hours. Do not infer either from scenic designation; no access guarantee is made.
Both current moments retained. Marshlands is a new historic-house moment placed before Fort Johnson using SCDNR’s campus approach and its cached coordinates. No interior access is claimed.
The cache provides no history of enslaved labor specific to Marshlands; its moment is limited to relocation and documented current institutional use.

Current first-shots claim is supported by SCDNR but replaced with the more specific 1861 Fort Sumter connection. Island battle and Kosciuszko details were cut for focus, not lack of evidence. Current story has no story-level motifs; output uses an empty array.

Overview deliberately remains below 200 words: cached sources lack the full road description, length, terrain and selection rationale. Added historical detail would displace the actual approach rather than repair that gap.
